item.title: Chemists develop AI tool to convert human ingenuity into life-enhancing enzymes
item.description: Many have voiced concerns that artificial intelligence will take jobs away from humans. But assistant professor of chemistry Zhongyue (John) Yang, along with his former doctoral student Qianzhen Shao (now a postdoc at Stanford) and other team members, has created an AI tool that aims to elevate the work that scientists do—not replace them. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Calling species 'invasive'—and culling them—isn't done lightly. But it matters to Australia's threatened species
item.description: It may sound abstract, but distinctions between "native," "introduced" or "invasive" species can often be life or death. Species considered invasive in Australia—such as European rabbits and feral pigs—are often culled, while most native animals are generally left alone. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ultracold atoms simulate hard-to-observe matter-antimatter pair production
item.description: According to quantum electrodynamics, the theory describing interactions between light and electrically charged particles, a sufficiently strong electric field can, in principle, convert some of its energy into particles and their antimatter partners. A particle's antimatter partner has the same mass and, for electrically charged particles, the opposite electric charge. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA-funded study reveals 4.1-billion-year-old history of pink Martian rock found in Sahara
item.description: Discovered in the vast Sahara Desert, the meteorite Teghaza 001 is over four billion years old and is confirmed to be a Martian rock via isotopic studies. This intriguing specimen reveals a volcanic history intertwined with water activity, indicating a complex water cycle on Mars. As researchers delve deeper into its origins, they are unraveling vital insights into the planet's early environmental conditions. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.description: Article URL: https://science.nasa.gov/mission/voyager/voyager-1/voyager-1-what-is-a-light-day/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50317429 Points: 61 # Comments: 28 Fuente: Hacker News - Portada.
item.dc:creator: geox

item.title: Four superconducting cables link two large quantum processors into one
item.description: As quantum computers grow more ambitious, many researchers believe the best way forward is to build them in multiple interconnected parts. In these modular designs, separate quantum processors are linked so they can work together as one larger machine. For this to happen, however, connections must carry fragile quantum information without destroying it. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Rare Iron Age Celtic helmet discovered in northeastern Poland far from its homeland
item.description: Around 2,400 years ago, at Łysa Góra in Poland, a group of people took a bronze helmet, crushed it, broke it into pieces and threw it into a pit with iron adzes and a scythe. Such helmets are sometimes found in lavish graves of the Celtic warrior elite, from Champagne, France, to Dürrnberg, Austria. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New gel fuel could make rocket and satellite propulsion easier to control
item.description: A kerosene-based gel developed by Concordia researchers could make rocket and satellite fuels easier to store and control. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists finally discover how a common gut bacterium can trigger colon cancer
item.description: Scientists at Johns Hopkins have uncovered a crucial missing link between a common gut bacterium and colorectal cancer, solving a mystery that has puzzled researchers for nearly two decades. The bacterium, Bacteroides fragilis, produces a toxin that damages the colon’s protective lining, triggers chronic inflammation, and promotes tumor formation. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: A mysterious 4,000-year-old wall is rewriting North Africa’s history
item.description: A remarkable 4,000-year-old defensive structure discovered in Morocco is rewriting what scientists thought they knew about ancient North African civilizations. The massive fortifications reveal unexpectedly sophisticated prehistoric societies and suggest that the region played a much greater role in Mediterranean history than previously recognized. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: España lidera un ranking europeo en el que no quería estar: el de los sistemas solares expuestos en internet
item.description: La transición energética, el auge de las renovables y la apuesta por la electrificación suponen una transformación tan profunda que no está exenta de riesgos. Tampoco sus instalaciones. Esto es lo que se desgrana de To See the Wind and the Sun , realizado por Modat Magnify, con la colaboración de Bouke van Laethem del Centro Nacional de Ciberseguridad de Países Bajos (NCSC-NL). Analizando países de la Unión Europea y candidatos a serlo y la EFTA, los investigadores han identificado más de 8.000 interfaces sin los mecanismos de seguridad necesarios, pertenecientes a instalaciones de renovables… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Alexandra Ramírez

item.title: Rare fossil discovery reveals new dinosaur species that specialized in eating fruit
item.description: Among the ravenous carnivores and lumbering herbivores that roamed the Cretaceous landscape, another kind of dinosaur was evolving that started to eat something else: the plants that began to flower and produce fruit. The discovery by paleontologists from Stony Brook University, Royal Ontario Museum (ROM) and the North Dakota Geological Survey reveals that a new species, Infernogallus jamesi—a type of small oviraptorosaur—had chewing muscles for mashing soft food, making it the first known dinosaur that specifically ate fruit. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists discover metals that defy the deep freeze at -424°F
item.description: Scientists have discovered a surprising mechanism that allows certain metals to resist cracking at temperatures as low as -253°C (-424°F), when similar materials typically become dangerously brittle. Instead of breaking, two experimental alloys reorganize their internal structures, creating new ways to absorb stress and remain flexible. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: In 1901,sponge divers off the Greek island of Antikythera recovered a gear from 2,000 years ago
item.description: In 1900, a remarkable discovery was made when divers stumbled upon the Antikythera Mechanism amidst a shipwreck in the Mediterranean Sea. This ancient artifact showcased astounding knowledge of astronomy and mechanical engineering dating back over 2,000 years. Researchers found it capable of calculating astronomical cycles and predicting eclipses, intertwining science with the cultural tapestry of ancient Greece. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Lifestyle Desk

item.title: In 2003, archaeologists in London found a tin pot nearly 2,000 years old full of face cream
item.description: In a remarkable find in 2003, archaeologists unveiled a cosmetic cream container dating back almost 2,000 years in London. Composed of animal fat, starch, and tin oxide, this ancient formula likely served as a moisturizer. Researchers painstakingly recreated the cream to explore its texture and look on the skin, shedding light on the beauty rituals of the past and our enduring human connection to history. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Lifestyle Desk

item.title: 'Molecular armor' can trap shape-matched planar molecules
item.description: A research team has designed and synthesized a molecular cage with an internal cavity by connecting two curved π-conjugated molecules face-to-face at three points. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 75,000-year-old Neanderthal may have been killed by a spear aimed at the heart
item.description: A Neanderthal who died 75,000 years ago may have been killed by a wooden spear deliberately aimed at the heart, revealing rare evidence of prehistoric violence. A circular hole in the shoulder blade suggests the weapon pierced the chest and caused a rapidly fatal injury. Surprisingly, the same individual had survived an earlier devastating facial injury, suggesting other Neanderthals provided care and support. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Nations commit to get nature goals back on track
item.description: The United Nations had warned that progress was insufficient to meet the goals of the 2030 target including protecting 30% of Earth’s land and oceans, tackling pollution and invasive species, and boosting money for conservation Publicado también por: The Hindu - International. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Hemos encontrado un pequeño pueblo en Cerdeña donde las mujeres tienen una vida excepcionalmente longeva
item.description: Durante décadas, los investigadores han estado buscando descifrar el secreto que hay en las llamadas "zonas azules", que no son más que regiones del planeta donde vivir muchos años (incluso más de 100) parece ser la norma y no la excepción. Uno de estos casos tan peculiares lo tenemos en la isla de Cerdeña (Italia) donde existe un área montañosa que fue identificada ya a principios de los 2000 por su inusual proporción de hombres centenarios. Un nuevo caso. Ahora, un nuevo estudio apunta a un pequeño municipio sardo, Bolotana, como una nueva y sorprendente "zona azul candidata", esta vez… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: José A. Lizana

item.title: Un estudio explica por qué en España 1 GW de centros de datos no se solucionará instalando simplemente 1 GW de renovables
item.description: Que los centros de datos necesitan una cantidad ingente de electricidad no es ninguna sorpresa. Estos “ vampiros energéticos ” suponen uno de los principales retos a los que se enfrentan los países que los van a albergar. En España, el Gobierno ha intentado abordar este desafío vinculando la expansión de los centros de datos a la generación renovable , de manera que no supongan un peaje altísimo que obligue al sistema eléctrico a recurrir a más generación fósil o a incrementar la presión sobre los precios. Sin embargo, y aunque se ha presentado recientemente un nuevo borrador mucho más suave… Fuente: Xataka.

item.title: AI is coming to construction sites. But does it make workers safer?
item.description: AI is flagging hazards on construction sites, but researchers say evidence that the technology prevents injuries remains limited. Fuente: CNBC - World.

item.title: A surprising vitamin A discovery is changing what scientists know about vision
item.description: Scientists at Johns Hopkins University have uncovered a surprising process that helps humans develop sharp vision before birth, challenging decades of assumptions about how the eye forms. Using miniature human retinas grown in the lab, researchers discovered that a vitamin A derivative and thyroid hormones work together to shape the foveola, the tiny region at the center of the retina responsible for our sharpest vision. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Spatial mapping reveals how human urogenital organs codevelop during organogenesis
item.description: A new study has mapped human urogenital development in its native spatial context, revealing how neighboring organs coordinate their development through cellular communication and molecular signaling during embryogenesis. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists smash oxygen nuclei to recreate matter from the Big Bang
item.description: Scientists have recreated a primordial state of matter from the dawn of the universe by colliding oxygen nuclei at nearly the speed of light. The surprising results show that this exotic substance can form in smaller, lower-energy collisions than previously demonstrated, challenging the known boundaries of early-universe physics. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists develop new system to boost prime editing in dicot plants
item.description: A new gene-editing system could make it easier for researchers to introduce precise genetic changes into crops such as tomatoes, soybeans and rapeseed. Developed by researchers in China, SmartPE improves prime editing efficiency in several dicot plants, addressing a major limitation of the technique. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Los familiares de las víctimas y los desaparecidos en el choque de trenes en Toledo exigen respuestas y un rendimiento de cuentas por el accidente. Mientras los investigadores continúan con las indagaciones, el ministro de Transportes de Pedro Sánchez, Óscar Puente, afirmó que no renunciará a su cargo, pese a las críticas. Fuente: France 24 - Español.

item.title: A simple blood test could reveal Alzheimer’s risk 10 years before symptoms
item.description: A major international study found that a simple blood test could help predict Alzheimer’s-related cognitive decline years before symptoms appear, with the highest-risk individuals facing a 38% chance of impairment within five years and an estimated 78% chance within 10 years. Scientists believe the discovery could pave the way for earlier intervention and future treatments designed to prevent Alzheimer’s before memory problems begin. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Figuring out where cosmic neutrinos come from is tricky—radio telescopes could help find 'ghost particles' origin
item.description: Neutrinos are funny little particles that weigh almost nothing, making them one of the universe's most elusive building blocks. They can come from objects as mundane as bananas and as exotic as supernovas—the exploding death throes of massive stars. Most neutrinos stream through space and pass through the Earth without interacting with anything. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Once again, NASA is asking for ideas to rescue Hubble from certain death
item.description: The space agency solicited ideas for reboosting Hubble four years ago, but they didn't go anywhere. Fuente: Ars Technica.

item.description: In the Texas Panhandle, two livestock guardian dogs patrol a herd of cattle grazing the Rita Blanca National Grasslands. Although their singular focus is protecting the herd from would-be predators, their presence may make them wildlife conservation allies. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New home for orangutans rescued from Indonesia's burning forests
item.description: Deep in a forest in Indonesian Borneo, conservationists open a cage. A female orangutan and her baby waste little time, clambering up the towering trees and disappearing into the canopy, safe at last. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: For many, striped bass fishing is a way of life. But the iconic species could face collapse
item.description: Striped bass fishing has been Bill Jakob's passion for more than 60 years, and he remembers an era when he'd spend all night casting his line into the crashing waves off Montauk and get eight or nine fish ranging up to 40 pounds (18 kilograms), a big catch by anyone's standards. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Chemists create disappearing tattoos: Here's the science behind how they work
item.description: How handy would it be if you could make your tattoos invisible for a job interview in the morning, and reveal them again for a party in the evening? This sounds like science fiction, but it may soon be reality. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Are narcissists multiplying or is the social media algorithm making them bolder? The answer in five stages
item.description: Social media doesn't necessarily reflect who you are, but it may intensify particular personality traits and confirm or even persuade you that your worst behavior is justified. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Hidden erosion: Study reveals soft mountain rock erodes three times faster than hard rock—with climate implications
item.description: A University of Massachusetts Amherst-led research team has discovered that weaker rock in mountain landscapes erodes three times faster than harder rock—even on gentler slopes—and is one of the main attributes governing mountain erosion. The finding also challenges our current understanding of the relationship between erosion and the release of carbon dioxide, and suggests that geologists and atmospheric scientists may be underestimating the CO₂ contributions coming from the Earth's rocky places. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Tiny photonic chip links telescopes together to view the universe in 'astonishing' detail
item.description: A tiny glass chip developed by researchers at Heriot-Watt University has linked two telescopes together to enable them to act as a single powerful instrument, marking an important step toward a new generation of astronomical technology. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: What the Cornell 7 sexual assault allegations reveal about how parents talk to their kids about rape
item.description: There is approximately 60 years of research on campus sexual assault and shelves full of books on young people's sexual experiences and behaviors, including their experiences with assault. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why it could be a bad idea to get AI to flirt for you
item.description: You finally started an online conversation with a stranger you find attractive, yet you don't really know what to say. They seem happy to talk, but you struggle to find the correct responses. You worry that their patience is growing thin. You pray for some guidance. Luckily, the solution could be just a few clicks away. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Hauntology examines how what happened in the past—and what didn't—informs the present
item.description: The spooky is a hugely popular phenomenon in British culture, demonstrated in what now seems like a month-long Halloween celebration, a rich tradition of horror cinema and a growing interest in the uncanny. But there are other manifestations of haunting. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How a 'tropical' shortcut could help particle collider experiments
item.description: Particle accelerators are expensive. Not just to build or to run, but also to predict the outcome of measurements obtained from them. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Por qué el dolor de espalda crónico se siente tan personal: el cerebro lo trata como parte de quiénes somos
item.description: Las personas que conviven con el dolor de espalda crónico saben bien que, de un modo u otro, se ha convertido en parte de su personalidad. Despiertan cada mañana atentos a las sensaciones del nuevo día, cancelan planes por los dolores, dejan de practicar deportes que adoraban o incluso de coger en brazos a sus propios hijos… Es mucho más que un simple dolor. De hecho, está tan sumamente arraigado a la personalidad que, según un nuevo estudio, activa zonas del cerebro relacionadas con la autoconciencia. Es un descubrimiento interesante tanto por dar explicación a algo que en cierto modo… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Azucena Martín

item.description: AmAmerica’s newest aerospace expo and air show – MAX POWER – is fast approaching, and NASA has announced key events beginning Friday, Nov. 6, and running through Sunday, Nov. 8, hosted on and near the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Through multiple park experiences at MAX POWER, NASA and a variety of external collaborators […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Novel chemical reaction expands options for building DNA-encoded libraries
item.description: Finding new drugs requires screening vast numbers of compounds to identify those that interact with a biological target. DNA-encoded libraries (DELs) help researchers explore these large collections by attaching a short DNA sequence to each molecule, acting as a molecular barcode that allows compounds with promising properties to be identified. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Survey reveals what students think about AI
item.description: College students say they use AI mostly for learning and don't use it to cut corners but think that their peers do, according to the inaugural Dartmouth AI Survey, a new multiyear survey on how AI is shaping students' learning and career readiness. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: UTe₂ reveals two flavors of superconductivity under extreme pressure
item.description: Quantum researchers are searching for a topological superconductor—a material that, if discovered, would allow major advances in quantum computing by combining two distinct "flavors" of superconductivity. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Christina Koch, astronauta y ganadora del premio Princesa de Asturias: “Siento nostalgia de la Luna”
item.description: La astronauta de Artemis II reflexionó sobre la exploración espacial; destacó la importancia de cuidar nuestro planeta y explicó por qué considera necesario avanzar hacia Marte Fuente: La Nación - El Mundo.

item.title: A decade of carbon dioxide data from space gets an upgrade
item.description: Every day, two NASA space instruments known as the Orbiting Carbon Observatory-2 and -3 (OCO-2 and OCO-3) capture more than a million observations of sunlight reflecting off Earth's surface. Using the physics of how light travels through the air, an algorithm converts these raw data into atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO₂) concentrations. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Using less politically charged language can 'lower the temperature' on DEI training
item.description: Replacing commonly used diversity, equity and inclusion-related terminology such as "belonging" with carefully matched alternative language may improve Republicans' favorability toward diversity training, according to new research from the ILR School. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Rediscovered 1935 recordings reveal earliest known spoken audio of endangered Louisiana Creole
item.description: The earliest spoken-word recordings of Louisiana Creole, a uniquely American language at risk of extinction, have been uncovered and analyzed for the first time, shedding light on a tongue that defined the docks and saloons of New Orleans for well over a century. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Drone-based AI system tracks cattle growth without stressful trips to scales
item.description: In beef cattle production, determining the ideal time to sell makes all the difference in a producer's costs. This is because, once an animal reaches its natural growth limit, it stops gaining weight significantly. From that point on, every additional day in a feedlot means spending money on feed without gaining meat in return. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Baldosas magnéticas autoensamblables podrían construir los hábitats espaciales del futuro
item.description: Baldosas magnéticas autoensamblables podrían construir los hábitats espaciales del futuro CNNESPANOL.CNN.COM Baldosas magnéticas autoensamblables podrían construir los hábitats espaciales del futuro | CNN Fuente: CNN en Español.

item.title: Twice as many plants and animals sold in wildlife trade as previously thought, says report
item.description: More than 100,000 species are traded globally, whether illegally smuggled, sold as ornaments or in fisheries, timber and fashion industries, study finds The number of plant and animal species in use or sold in the wildlife trade is more than twice as high as previously thought, researchers have discovered. A study, published in Science Advances , warns that there are huge gaps in global assessments of how wildlife is traded, and that past estimates have failed to keep up with changes such as the boom in the online exotic pet trade , where sellers offering to post spider eggs across the world… Fuente: The Guardian - Environment.
item.dc:creator: Rebecca Ratcliffe

item.title: Q&A: Deep learning–enhanced air quality monitoring achieved using satellite data
item.description: A doctoral dissertation by Andrea Porcheddu, MSc in the field of Technical Physics will be examined at the Faculty of Science, Forestry and Technology, Kuopio campus. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Global wildlife trade is twice previous species estimates, but major data gaps suggest true scale is even larger
item.description: More than 107,000 species are used and traded worldwide, more than double previous estimates, according to new research that suggests the true scale may be far greater due to major gaps in trade and wildlife collection data. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 17th-century sleuths in the dock for witchcraft and wizardry
item.description: Magical versions of today's private investigators found themselves on the wrong side of the law in one English city some 400 years ago, according to research by a University of Southampton historian. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ancient copper mine hints that Iberia played an important role in Bronze Age trade networks
item.description: Copper is essential for making bronze, which shaped tools, weapons and ornaments across Bronze Age Europe. While many Bronze Age mines have been identified throughout Europe, researchers are still trying to pin down which of them were most active at different times and how far their copper traveled. New research, published in the journal Antiquity, suggests that a series of mines in modern-day Spain and Portugal may have been an important source of copper in the Late Bronze Age, with some of that copper ending up as far away as Scandinavia. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A gamma-ray powerhouse's smoking gun? Gas trail points to microquasar jets
item.description: In 2016, a binary star system emitting unusually strong gamma rays was discovered in our galactic neighborhood. Now, astronomers have found the smoking gun, or rather, a smoking trail of cool molecular gas that suggests jets emanating from a microquasar—one of the few known outside the Milky Way—are responsible. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The bonus that makes employees more committed
item.description: Offer your employees money to quit and the ones who say no will work harder as a result. Researchers at the University of Waterloo, Wilfrid Laurier University and McMaster University set out to test whether pay-to-quit programs work as intended. Their results confirmed they do and revealed a benefit that nobody anticipated. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Different transcription systems shape chromatin behavior in distinct nuclear regions
item.description: Inside the cell nucleus, DNA is wrapped around histone proteins to form nucleosomes, which are further organized into chromatin. Chromatin has traditionally been divided into transcriptionally active euchromatin and relatively inactive heterochromatin. However, chromatin is not a fixed structure. Nucleosomes continuously move within the nucleus, and this motion is closely related to the physical organization and function of the genome. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Supercharged 'molecule highway' membrane that speeds water transport could transform industrial processing
item.description: New membrane technology delivering faster and more precise molecule separation could improve the efficiency and sustainability of energy-intensive industrial processes—from purifying chemicals and recovering valuable resources to producing sustainable fuels. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Pulling the strings: How stem cells in the developing fruit fly brain organize their DNA from outside the nucleus
item.description: Cells are very particular about the proper locations of their contents. For example, DNA is packaged in the nucleus in a highly specific way, but researchers are still trying to understand how this happens. For stem cells in the brain of a larval fruit fly—a model organism used to study processes such as early development—the DNA is organized so that the center of each strand, called the centromere, is at the top of the nucleus. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How fish schools swim in sync may come down to following one influential neighbor
item.description: Fish schools are a marvel of navigation. They move in concert without any one fish leading the way. Instead, their coordinated movements arise from individual fish continually adjusting their movements based on their neighbors. But how much of this social information each fish processes at once is less well understood. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Discovery of bromochloropyrene reveals unexpected biological properties
item.description: Environmental pollutants containing chlorine or bromine have been widely studied, but compounds containing both elements have remained largely unexplored. Researchers have now detected bromochloropyrene in industrial soils and harbor sediments, investigated its breakdown under simulated sunlight, and measured its activity through a biological receptor linked to toxic effects. The findings reveal distinct environmental and biological properties, highlighting the need to investigate other mixed-halogen pollutants and improve future environmental monitoring and risk assessment. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Researchers create light-activated cages for 'protein killer' molecules
item.description: Researchers have created a molecular "cage" that keeps protein-degrading drug molecules inactive until they are exposed to low-energy red light. The technology, called RuPHOTACs, controls when and where these molecules become active, which could help scientists develop treatments that destroy specific proteins while limiting unwanted effects elsewhere. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope Captures Eerie Cat’s Head
item.description: Intricate structures within the Cat’s Head Nebula are illuminated in this mid-infrared view from NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope released on Oct. 29, 2026. The distinctive “cat’s head” shape of the nebula was likely sculpted over time by the intense ultraviolet radiation and winds from massive stars in the Carina Nebula. As this stellar feedback […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Grades are not comparable across schools in Sweden, says researcher
item.description: Grades from compulsory school determine which pupils are accepted into popular upper secondary programs. A new thesis from Uppsala University shows that pupils at for-profit independent schools have, on average, higher grades than would statistically be expected given their backgrounds. The findings suggest that grading is more generous in independent schools and that the differences in grades may give pupils from high-income households a greater advantage in the competition for places at upper secondary school, at the expense of other pupils. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Quantum skyrmions outlast entanglement, hinting at more resilient networks
item.description: Quantum networks could one day connect quantum computers into more powerful systems and enable new forms of secure communication. But a fundamental obstacle stands in the way: Quantum information is extraordinarily fragile, and the entanglement between particles of light on which such networks would depend is easily disrupted. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists find that a 10-millisecond flash could help build more sensitive gas sensors
item.description: Nitrogen dioxide is a harmful gas that requires sensitive detection. Researchers used intense light pulses lasting 10 milliseconds to make molybdenum disulfide flakes and anchor isolated metal atoms in one step. Adding platinum improved the material's room-temperature response to nitrogen dioxide, reaching 100.8% at 400 parts per billion and a detection limit of 17.2 parts per billion. This approach could support advanced gas sensors and applications in catalysis and energy technologies. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Personal stories offer new insights into stuttering therapy, researchers find
item.description: Traditional speech-language therapy for people who stutter has largely operated under a medical model focused on eliminating dysfluency—breaks in the normal rhythm of speech. But for Rodney Gabel, a professor of speech-language pathology at Binghamton University, and Ladan Khoshbin, a doctoral student in Binghamton's Community Research and Action program, true progress in stuttering research begins with listening to people's stories. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why do terrorist attacks seem so predictable in hindsight?
item.description: "How could our society have let this happen?" Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Customizable nanoparticles show potential for delivering personalized cancer vaccines
item.description: A nanoscale particle with a unique structure, developed at MIT, holds potential as a customizable delivery vehicle for personalized cancer vaccines. The backbone of the vaccine is a modified, harmless bacteriophage called M13, which forms a nanofiber that can be coated with cancer antigens. By precisely controlling the density of those cancer proteins, the researchers found that they could create a vaccine that prevents the development of colon tumors in mice. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: What happened this month at the European Space Agency? (October 2026)
item.description: Video: 00:04:30 October was a month of discoveries and milestones. ESA’s Rosalind Franklin rover team trained in Spain’s desert, preparing for Mars. Our Smile mission captured the full ring of northern lights around Earth, while Mars Express uncovered new clues about a giant Martian cloud. ESA astronaut Sophie Adenot returned to Earth after 237 days in space, and Hera captured its first images of the asteroids it will study to help protect our planet. Meanwhile, ESA welcomed thousands of visitors for Open Days and teamed up with Pokémon to bring space science to new audiences. Here’s a look… Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: NASA Explores Potential Commercial Servicing for Hubble Telescope
item.description: NASA issued a Request for Information Oct. 29 to learn more about industry capabilities for in-space servicing to support the agency’s Hubble Space Telescope. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Snowfall and clouds may slow East Antarctic ice loss in a warmer world
item.description: A new modeling study, published in the journal Nature Climate Change, suggests that the East Antarctic Ice Sheet may be more resilient to extreme long-term warming than previously estimated. Increased snowfall, greater cloud cover and changes in atmospheric circulation could partially offset ice loss—even under very high carbon dioxide concentrations. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New research challenges long-held beliefs about Robert Burns and Jamaica
item.description: A new study by academics at the University of Glasgow provides the most detailed analysis to date of Robert Burns' connections with Jamaica and relationship to the Atlantic slavery system. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA's Voyager 1 conserves power, resolves brief communications pause
item.description: NASA's Voyager team is celebrating two recent developments with the Voyager 1 spacecraft: In September, they successfully completed a months-long effort to stretch the spacecraft's diminishing power supply. Then, on Oct. 20, an unexpected loss of communication with the spacecraft resolved itself after 48 hours, before the team sent commands to the spacecraft to troubleshoot the issue. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The genetic cost of being a lazy parent ... if you're a cuckoo finch
item.description: African cuckoo finches (Anomalospiza imberbis) are very deceptive birds, or at least the mothers are. They sneak into the nests of other birds, such as prinias and cisticolas, to lay their eggs, then slip away and leave the hosts to raise the chicks. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Week in images: 26-30 October 2026 Discover our week through the lens Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: Irlanda, un refugio para los estadounidenses en contra de Trump
item.description: Miles de estadounidenses han decidido dejarlo todo y abandonar su país para instalarse en Irlanda en busca de libertad y mejores condiciones de vida ante las políticas del gobierno de Donald Trump. Entre ellos hay investigadores, empresarios y estudiantes. Solo el año pasado, alrededor de 10.000 estadounidenses llegaron al país europeo y cerca de un centenar solicitó asilo, alegando persecución política, racial o por motivos de orientación sexual e identidad de género. Reportaje de Chloé Domat, Sophie Guignon y Merlin Ferret para France 24. Fuente: France 24 - Español.
item.dc:creator: Chloé Domat

item.title: Marine fossils in Colombia reveal possible evolutionary transition without mass extinction
item.description: A remarkably diverse fossil ecosystem in central Colombia that preserves an unusual overlap between survivors of older Jurassic groups and newer Cretaceous lineages has led researchers at McGill University and the Centro de Investigaciones Paleontológicas (CIP) to recognize a new pattern of large-scale evolutionary transition, one that does not include mass extinctions. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Award-winning research helps companies keep products where they're needed most
item.description: Before a stick of deodorant reaches a consumer's bathroom counter, it moves through a complex supply chain. Raw materials and packaging components are sourced, assembled into a finished product and shipped through warehouses and distribution centers before finally reaching a store shelf. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: JWST reveals a distant galaxy that may let most of its ionizing radiation escape
item.description: Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) have found evidence that a distant, exceptionally blue galaxy may allow most of its ionizing radiation to escape into space. Known as EBG-1, the gravitationally lensed galaxy is seen at a redshift of 9.244, about 530 million years after the Big Bang. The paper was posted to the arXiv preprint server on Oct. 16. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA's TRACERS first results offer peek into violent magnetic process
item.description: NASA's TRACERS (Tandem Reconnection and Cusp Electrodynamics Reconnaissance Satellites) mission has gathered its first clues to how space weather affects Earth's magnetic field. In a new paper published in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Space Physics, researchers break down how these interactions work after analyzing initial observations from the first year of the mission. Fuente: Phys.org.

NatGeo is always a good read bu... Ver más Samara Dyva Fuente: National Geographic.

item.title: Extraterrestrial detection inspired by firefly communications could distinguish alien signals from pulsars
item.description: When we think of extraterrestrial intelligence that might be out there among the stars, we tend to think of creatures not too unlike us, though maybe with gray skin, probably bald and with big black eyes. We focus on the familiar, humanoids. But there are many intelligent species on Earth that are nonhumanoid: dolphins, crows, pigs and—with swarm if not individual intelligence—ants and bees. The film "Arrival" conceived of hexapod beings more capable than humans and with a more sophisticated communication system. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Resident experience matters in estimating neighborhood walkability, study shows
item.description: Walking has been shown to improve the overall health of a community and can predict the prevalence of chronic diseases, such as obesity, diabetes and cardiovascular disease, according to the World Health Organization. Because of this, city planners assess neighborhoods' walkability, which measures how built environments support walking, when planning improvements. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Flying‑foxes are starving. Why are we still responding one crisis at a time?
item.description: Once again, Australia's flying-foxes are in trouble. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Confirming altermagnetism: A geometric twist offers experimental proof
item.description: For decades, physicists recognized only two types of magnetism that occur in materials without external influence: ferromagnetism and antiferromagnetism. In findings published in Science, a team led by the U.S. Department of Energy's SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory has delivered conclusive experimental proof of a third magnetic phase called altermagnetism. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Type 2 diabetes breakthrough as 54% achieve remission in just 6 months
item.description: A promising new study suggests that more than half of younger adults with type 2 diabetes could achieve remission in just six months through a combination of a low-calorie diet and structured exercise. Researchers found that 54% of participants under age 45 who followed an intensive diet and exercise program achieved remission, compared with just 4% receiving usual care. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Long-standing Indigenous practice of adding shells to sand helps young clams withstand ocean acidification
item.description: New research from the University of California, Davis, reveals why adding crushed shells to beach sand helps protect shell-making animals—such as clams, oysters and mussels—from the detrimental effects of ocean acidification. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Burrowing shrimp are on the move in a mudflat near you
item.description: Burrowing shrimp are a pest well known to shellfish growers. These pale-bodied creatures excavate mud as they dig into the ground, creating piles of sediment that suffocate oysters and clams growing on the surface. In estuaries on the West Coast, shrimp beds reach densities of hundreds of shrimp per square meter, but the boundaries of the beds change. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Physicists created a tiny universe and watched time emerge without a clock
item.description: Scientists have created a miniature universe in the laboratory that could help answer one of the biggest mysteries in physics: What is time, and where does it come from? Using 24,000 ultracold atoms, a University of Birmingham researcher built an isolated quantum system that repeatedly expands and contracts, mimicking the Big Bang and a possible Big Crunch. Remarkably, the experiment showed that time could emerge from changes happening inside the system, without relying on an external clock. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Unusual quantum states in six-layer graphene offer clues to superconductivity
item.description: Graphene, a material consisting of a sheet of carbon atoms arranged in a honeycomb pattern, has proved promising for various technological applications. Materials in which several layers of graphene are stacked together can exhibit different advantageous properties. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Reexamining sexual and species recognition in butterflies: The Partner-Hazard Space framework
item.description: Generally, intra- and intersexual interactions have been considered qualitatively different processes. However, same-sex sexual behavior is widespread in the animal kingdom, challenging this assumption. Recently, a hypothesis was proposed that regards territorial contests in butterflies, in which two males chase each other without apparent physical attack, as an initial phase of mating behavior. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The asteroid killed the dinosaurs. Why did crocodiles survive?
item.description: Scientists may have solved a 66-million-year-old mystery: how crocodiles survived the asteroid that wiped out the dinosaurs. A sweeping analysis of fossils and ancient climates suggests that their preference for warm environments placed them in tropical refuges that remained habitable even after the catastrophic impact. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Asking teachers to set high expectations leads to more detailed feedback and reveals subtle bias, study finds
item.description: Prompting teachers to communicate high expectations and confidence in students' potential leads them to give more detailed feedback, according to a new study led by Yasemin Copur-Gencturk, Ph.D., a professor of education at USC Rossier and co-director of the USC STEM Center; Ian Thacker, Ph.D., an associate professor of educational psychology at The University of Texas at San Antonio; and Joseph Cimpian, Ph.D., a professor of economics and education policy at New York University. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A computer scientist breaks through a limit that stood since 1996
item.description: A computer scientist has achieved a breakthrough in a nearly 25-year-old problem involving how computers calculate distances across enormous networks. The new algorithm delivers more reliable estimates for closely connected points without sacrificing speed, overcoming a longstanding limitation of earlier methods. Its secret lies in a smarter way of sampling network connections at multiple scales. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Rocket Report: Winter is coming for Themis; Cowboy Space adds iron to the fire
item.description: It's been a good week for ULA with a big NASA contract and Vulcan nearing return-to-flight. Fuente: Ars Technica.

item.title: Most influencers should swear off profanity
item.description: If you spend time watching online videos, you might feel like covering your ears. For some influencers, dropping f-bombs and other swear words is part of their brand, and their followers embrace it. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Cuando pienses que la cera de tus oídos es molesta y asquerosa, piensa que sería peor tener insectos ahí dentro
item.description: El cerumen que se acumula en nuestros oídos para muchas personas es asqueroso e innecesario, puesto que puede generar tapones que nos generan una disminución en la capacidad de escucha. Pero aunque para un buen grupo de la población la cera de los oídos es sinónimo de una falta de higiene, para la biología es un sofisticado sistema de seguridad biomecánico que evita que los insectos colonicen nuestro oído. Dos propiedades. Tras estudiar el cerumen de nuestros oídos, los investigadores han entendido la compleja mecánica que hay detrás, puesto que se ha visto que tiene dos propiedades que… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: José A. Lizana

item.title: Hubble reveals a stunning twist in how the universe emerged from darkness
item.description: A surprising discovery by astronomers using the Hubble Space Telescope is challenging a leading explanation for how the early universe emerged from a dense fog of hydrogen roughly 13 billion years ago. Scientists once believed powerful winds from exploding stars helped radiation escape galaxies and clear that cosmic fog, but new observations reveal that these winds actually block radiation instead. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists reveal a hidden snakebite crisis killing up to 513,000 people a year
item.description: A startling new study suggests that venomous snakebites are killing far more people worldwide than official statistics indicate, with an estimated 274,000 to 513,000 deaths every year. Researchers found that as many as 7 million people could suffer snake envenoming annually, while more than 800,000 survivors are left with long-term disabilities. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Why some “lower-risk” childhood cancers turn deadly
item.description: Scientists have uncovered hidden aggressive cancer cells in children whose tumors were previously considered lower risk, revealing why some cases of rhabdomyosarcoma become unexpectedly deadly. The discovery could help doctors identify dangerous tumors earlier and develop personalized treatments that improve survival while reducing unnecessary chemotherapy. Fuente: ScienceDaily.
